_readme: One entry per partner. Edit here, then run `python3 partners/build.py` to regenerate partners/<slug>/index.html and partners/index.html. Empty strings and empty lists are fine: the page simply omits that section. In what/why/funding/serves/offers you can write [label](https://url) for an inline link; it renders as a link that opens in a new tab. Fields: slug (URL), name, url (their site), tagline (one line), tags (3), cohort (partnership years shown on the page, e.g. '2026–2031'), term (e.g. '2026–2031'), led_by, serves, offers (list of short items), what (1 paragraph, their words), why (1 paragraph, ASF's words), quote {text, who}, funding (what they have accomplished during the partnership, 1 paragraph), numbers (list of {value, label}), donate, contact, photo (path relative to the partner's folder, or empty).

partners.name: Black E.S.T.E.E.M.
partners.tagline: Hands-on STEM, leadership, and entrepreneurship programs building confidence and career pathways for Black girls ages 8–16 across the GTA.
offers: Hands-on STEM workshops and camps
Leadership and mentorship programs
Entrepreneurship training for teens
Exposure to Black women in science, technology, engineering, and business
partners.what: Black E.S.T.E.E.M. (Entrepreneurs, Scientists, Technicians, Engineers, Economists, Mathematicians) runs hands-on programs where Black girls build, code, experiment, pitch, and lead. Workshops and camps are paired with a network of mentors drawn from the fields the girls are being introduced to.
partners.why: The organization runs on a "for us, by us" principle: founded by an educator, rooted in the community they serve, and focused on access, opportunity, and long-term economic mobility. By their own reporting they have grown from 50 girls to a network of more than 500, with 98% program completion and alumni going on to post-secondary STEM, on a modest budget. They list partnerships with Apple, Microsoft, the Ontario Science Centre, and local universities.

partners.name: MIND Program
partners.tagline: Free homemade meals and on-site food banks, delivered through frontline agencies to Torontonians for whom hunger stands in the way of healing.
offers: Free homemade meals delivered to community housing sites
On-site food banks
Partnerships with frontline agencies already working in each building
partners.what: MIND Program (Moving In New Directions) brings food to where people already are. They work through frontline organizations in Toronto Community Housing buildings in Scarborough, delivering free homemade meals and running on-site food banks. The people they reach include refugees, seniors, and low-income housed and unhoused individuals and families. The meals are cooked, not pre-packaged, and the program is built around the dignity of the people receiving them.
partners.why: Almost [one in four Ontario households](https://www.publichealthontario.ca/-/media/Documents/F/25/food-insecurity-food-affordability.pdf) experiences food insecurity. MIND's answer is a partnership rather than another food bank. They work with frontline medical, mental health, and social service teams that lack the facilities, certifications, or budgets to feed the people they serve. MIND reports that meals at one harm-reduction hub tripled the number of people seeking its services, and that supply partnerships have cut their cost per meal by three-quarters. Their director has deliberately kept the organization from "chasing the same piece of pie." They were recently featured in Toronto Foundation's [Good to Give Guide](https://torontofoundation.ca/goodtogive2026/#charities).

numbers.label: cost per meal, down from $4.86 in 2024

partners.name: Oasis Youth Care Programs
partners.tagline: Transitional housing and wrap-around support helping Black and racialized youth in Halton and Peel move from homelessness to stable, permanent homes.
offers: Oasis House transitional homes in Oakville
A resource centre for youth not in residence
Case management, life skills, and housing search support
A path to permanent housing, with follow-up after move-out
partners.what: Oasis Youth Care Programs runs transitional homes for young people who have nowhere stable to live. By their own account, they surround that housing with the support it takes to leave it well. Oasis is based in Oakville and serves Halton and Peel, suburbs where youth homelessness is real but services are thin.
partners.why: Oasis describe themselves as Halton's only intentionally Black-led, Black-serving youth housing program, and they meet an urgent need: youth aging out of child protection with nowhere stable to go. Their model is the evidence-based Foyer approach, which pairs housing with mentorship and skills rather than treating a bed as the whole answer. They report that 90% of their residents move on to permanent housing without re-entering the shelter system. By their count, demand far exceeds capacity: 78 referrals over six years against room for 21.

partners.name: Power To Girls Foundation
partners.tagline: School-based mentorship, leadership, and wellness programming that builds sisterhood and self-worth for Black girls and young women across the GTA.
offers: School-based mentorship circles
Leadership and wellness programming
Annual conferences and summer opportunities
The MY Power app
Youth-led research on the experiences of Black girls in Ontario schools
partners.what: Power To Girls runs mentorship and leadership programs inside schools, where Black girls spend most of their day and where, too often, they are overlooked or over-disciplined. Programs are built around sisterhood: small circles, consistent mentors, and space to be a whole person.
partners.why: Few programs in the city are both gender-specific and culturally relevant. Power To Girls is designed with the girls themselves, and girls who were mentored come back as mentors. By their own count they have reached more than 10,000 girls across the GTA since 2013. They run in roughly eleven schools, with fifteen more on the waiting list, and hold an annual conference of 300 or more. They have also published their own research with 245 Black girls on their experience of Ontario schools.

partners.name: Sawubona Africentric Circle of Support
partners.tagline: Culturally responsive caregiver support, workshops, and advocacy for Black families raising children and adults with disabilities.
partners.led_by: Sherron Grant and Clovis Grant, Co-founders
offers: Peer support circles for caregivers
One-to-one help navigating services and funding
Workshops and a caregiver toolkit in English and French
Community events that bring isolated families together
Advocacy within the disability and education systems
partners.what: Sawubona is a Zulu greeting that means "I see you." The organization was founded by parents who found that disability services were not built with Black families in mind, and who wanted a place where families like theirs could be seen. Through peer support circles, one-to-one navigation support, workshops, and community gatherings, they equip caregivers to advocate for their family members inside systems that are often hard to move.
partners.why: Their co-founders are parents of an adult child with special needs, and they have run the organization as unpaid volunteers while steadily professionalizing it. They report reaching more than 300 caregivers, and they have completed an external evaluation, written a five-year plan, and earned provincial and national caregiving awards. The caregivers named the organization and set its agenda; it is theirs.

partners.name: Black Creek Community Farm
partners.tagline: An urban agricultural centre rooted in Toronto's Jane and Finch neighbourhood, engaging diverse communities through sustainable food.
offers: A working farm inside the city
Fresh, affordable produce for the neighbourhood
Youth and community programming on the land
partners.what: Black Creek Community Farm is a working farm in Jane and Finch, one of Toronto's most diverse and least-served neighbourhoods. They grow food for the community, employ and train local residents and youth, and use the land as a gathering place for education, culture, and food justice work.
partners.why: Black Creek Community Farm has strong, dynamic leadership, a community kitchen, a real focus on accessibility, and a breadth of programming backed by early revenue-generating work. Few organizations combine all of that on a single site, and it is led from within the neighbourhood it serves.
partners.funding: The farm reported growing 22,000 pounds of produce in a recent year, distributed through their sliding-scale Harvest Share program and farm stands. Their Urban Harvest partnership with the City redistributed more than 2,900 kg of food to local food banks and programs, reaching nearly 700 households. They have launched a Land Stewardship Program rooted in Indigenous and diasporic knowledge, and a Youth Farm Residency for Black, Indigenous, and racialized youth from Jane-Finch. They have also joined the Nourish Leadership Anchor Cohort on food and health.

partners.name: Community Justice Collective
partners.tagline: Legal support for community organizers and social justice movements across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area.
offers: Legal advice and representation for organizers and movements
Know-your-rights education
Support for tenant and community campaigns
partners.what: Community Justice Collective is a movement lawyering organization. They provide legal support to the organizers, tenant groups, and grassroots campaigns that larger legal clinics cannot take on. They do it as a partner in the work, not a service provider at arm's length.
partners.why: The people CJC defends are the ones institutions with money or power try to slow down through the legal process: tenant unions, encampment residents, mutual-aid groups, land defenders. They are a small team working from a donated office, and by their own account they have never lost a client they started with. They report having beaten dozens of eviction and encampment charges. CJC decides for themselves whom they represent and how, and that independence is exactly why it works.
partners.funding: According to their annual reports, CJC has acted as counsel for rent strikes across the city. One precedent-setting win at 1440–1442 Lawrence Avenue West reversed an illegal eviction and compelled the landlord to fix the building. They report having influenced provincial bail-reform legislation. They have also partnered with U of T's Faculty of Law on a legal-tech tool for marginalized communities, mentored 13 aspiring lawyers, and launched Counsel Call, which became Canada's top "How To" podcast. They used part of our grant to pay tenant leaders to become organizers, and are now expanding into workers' rights.

partners.name: Homeless Connect Toronto
partners.tagline: Coordinates "one-stop-shop" events connecting people at risk of or experiencing homelessness with the supports they need.
offers: Large one-day service events bringing dozens of providers under one roof
Health care, ID, housing, employment, and legal supports on site
A volunteer base drawn from across the city
partners.what: Homeless Connect Toronto runs events built around a single day. Someone who is homeless or close to it can see a doctor, replace lost ID, talk to a housing worker, get a haircut, and sit down for a meal. The idea is to bring the system to the person, once, in one place, instead of asking them to navigate it alone. Smaller Community Connect events and the Everyday Connect portal extend that through the year.
partners.why: Homeless Connect Toronto understands its niche and does not try to replicate what others do: the connection between a person and the services that already exist. Their peer-connector program is run entirely by people with lived experience of homelessness, and their director's stated goal is that everyone who works there is sustainably employed. They are lean, collaborative, and polished well beyond their resources.
partners.funding: By their 2024 annual report, Homeless Connect's October 2024 one-stop-shop served a record 1,240 guests with 339 volunteers and 322 service providers from 67 organizations. PeerConnectTO has trained three groups of peer workers with lived experience of homelessness. The organization is also part of a St. Michael's study on whether peer support improves health outcomes. They ran matching campaigns around our grant and in 2024 secured $69,337 in new grants alongside $210,000 in renewed commitments.

partners.name: ENAGB Indigenous Youth Agency
partners.tagline: Cultural, employment, life-skills, and wellness programs designed by and for Indigenous youth ages 12–29 in Toronto.
offers: Cultural programming and land-based learning
Employment and life-skills training
Holistic wellness and recreation
An EarlyON program for Indigenous families
An annual cultural festival and competition powwow
partners.what: ENAGB (Eshkiniigjik Naandwechigegamig, Aabiish Gaa Binjibaaying) is an Indigenous-led youth agency in Toronto, working with young people aged 12 to 29 and, through its EarlyON program, with families of children under six. Their programs are built to grow self-esteem, confidence, skills, and self-determination, with culture at the centre.
partners.why: ENAGB is youth-led as well as youth-serving. Through a Youth Council with real authority, the young people they work with have a say in how the agency runs and where it focuses. The programming reflects it: culture, ceremony, and land-based learning sit alongside employment and life-skills work rather than being added on. They have since grown from a largely volunteer-run program into a city-wide agency without losing that youth-centred character.
partners.funding: ENAGB has opened a West End location and runs land-based learning and ceremony at Memtigwaake Kinomaage Maawnjiding, a 2.7-acre cultural site on the Humber River. They secured $1 million over four years from the MLSE Foundation, and a $900,000 commitment from Sun Life for play-based programming. In 2026 they launched a large-scale competition powwow at Woodbine Park. The grassroots agency we met in 2021 is now a city-wide one.

partners.name: Maggie's Toronto Sex Workers Action Project
partners.tagline: Canada's oldest sex-worker justice initiative, offering wrap-around services and life-affirming care across Toronto and the GTA.
offers: Drop-in and outreach services
Harm reduction supplies and support
Peer-led programming and advocacy
partners.what: Maggie's is run by and for sex workers. They provide harm reduction, drop-in support, outreach, and advocacy grounded in the principle that sex workers are the experts on their own safety and their own lives. They have done this work in Toronto for decades, through changes in law and in public opinion.
partners.why: Maggie's serves one of the most neglected and vulnerable communities in the city, and advocates for the people within it who have the least choice. They are a small agency that takes on big things, and they have kept doing it through everything the last few years have thrown at them.
partners.funding: Maggie's unionized in 2021. After a 2023 fire caused at least $500,000 in damage to their main office, they kept their drop-in, outreach, and harm-reduction work running through major operational changes. They secured $850,000 over five years from the Public Health Agency of Canada.

partners.name: The Reading Partnership
partners.tagline: Builds literacy programs and resources for families and children in the Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park community of Scarborough.
offers: Parent-led early literacy programs
Reading resources and books for the home
Community events built around reading
partners.what: The Reading Partnership works on the belief that parents are a child's first teachers. In Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park, they train and support parents to build reading into daily life, put books into homes, and run programs that make literacy a community project rather than a school-only one.
partners.why: Prevention is the point: better literacy leads to better outcomes in everything else. Their model is flexible, following families between in-person, online, and asynchronous programming as their housing changes, and they feed families so they can take part. The organization ran for twelve years on a shared platform and then a trusteeship before becoming an independent charity, chronically underfunded and overlooked.
partners.funding: The Reading Partnership launched their 2024–2027 strategic plan and a research collaboration with the Canadian Children's Literacy Foundation on the reading journeys of Black children in Canada. Camesha Cox was inducted into the Scarborough Walk of Fame and named an Ashoka Fellow. They used our grant as a match for their year-end appeal, raising $43,641.91 by Camesha's account. Supporters told her the match made them give more, and she has since shared the approach with every partner we fund.

numbers.label: raised with a matched year-end appeal
TD Ready Challenge grant to scale nationally

partners.name: Toronto Alliance to End Homelessness
partners.tagline: A community-based collective-impact initiative working toward a Toronto where homelessness is rare, brief, and non-recurring.
offers: Coordination across agencies, funders, and government
Data and advocacy for a housing-first system
A platform for people with lived experience to shape policy
partners.what: The Toronto Alliance to End Homelessness brings together the agencies, advocates, and people with lived experience who make up Toronto's homelessness response. They push for a system that ends homelessness rather than managing it. Their work is coordination, data, and advocacy, the connective tissue that individual shelters and programs cannot build alone.
partners.why: TAEH is deliberately not funded by the City, because they advise the City. They are the formally recognized non-Indigenous Community Advisory Board on housing and homelessness. A paid caucus of people with lived experience sits inside every decision, and an anti-oppression framework shapes how the whole sector works with TAEH.
partners.funding: In November 2024 the City procured TAEH, with the Infrastructure Institute, to support applicants to the new $15 million Community Housing Pre-Development Fund. The work helps newer organizations develop rental and supportive housing. Their pre-budget submission to the federal government set out specific recommendations on housing funds, refugee settlement, and mental-health funding for homelessness services.

partners.name: Toronto Black Farmers
partners.tagline: A collective of urban farmers and growers building a community food hub focused on food sovereignty, justice, and access to clean food.
offers: Urban growing sites and a community food hub
Training for new Black farmers and growers
Culturally relevant produce for the community
partners.what: Toronto Black Farmers and Food Growers Collective grows food, trains growers, and builds the infrastructure of a community food hub rooted in Black food traditions. Their work is about sovereignty as much as supply: who owns the land, who grows the food, and who decides what the community eats.
partners.why: Toronto Black Farmers are excellent at the thing itself: growing good, locally grown, accessible food and teaching people to grow their own. Founders Jacqueline and Noel are among the most visible advocates for food justice in the city. It is a small organization doing front-line work with unusual integrity.
partners.funding: Toronto Black Farmers now provide produce year-round at their Downsview Park farm stand, and through the summer at the Afro-Caribbean Farmers Market. Since our partnership began they have added workshops, hands-on training, and youth farming programs.

partners.name: Thunder Woman Healing Lodge Society
partners.tagline: Trauma-informed, culturally grounded services and housing for First Nations, Inuit, and Métis 2SLGBTQIA+ women exiting the justice system.
offers: A temporary healing lodge, operating now, with housing and cultural support
Daughters of the Earth, a 16-week day program for women on probation or bail
Help accessing subsidized housing, financial supports, and life-skills programming
The permanent healing lodge in Scarborough, under construction
partners.what: Thunder Woman Healing Lodge Society is building Toronto's first healing lodge for Indigenous women and 2SLGBTQIA+ people leaving prison: a place to live, heal, and reconnect with culture rather than a halfway house. The permanent lodge is a six-storey building at 2217 Kingston Road in Scarborough, with 12 lodge beds and 12 affordable transitional units. It is not yet open. In the meantime the society runs a temporary lodge and community programs. Their services are designed by Indigenous women and grounded in ceremony, community, and the understanding that incarceration is one chapter of a longer story.
partners.why: The organization is strong, grounded in Indigenous culture and ceremony, and no-nonsense in how they work. When COVID pushed the lodge's original timeline out by years, they did not wait. They pivoted to smaller, local services so they could keep serving women in the meantime, and have never stopped.
partners.funding: When we first partnered in 2021 the lodge was a plan on a piece of land. The society opened a temporary healing lodge in a City-provided house in December 2022, and added a garden suite there in 2024. They launched Daughters of the Earth, and began developing Indigikwe, a social enterprise that will train up to 24 women a year. Building permits for the permanent lodge were issued in March 2025, and construction and fundraising for the final capital gap continue.

partners.name: Wanasah
partners.tagline: A non-profit mental-health agency addressing the urgent needs of Black youth and their families in Regent Park and surrounding downtown Toronto neighbourhoods.
offers: Counselling and therapy by Black clinicians
Family and community support
Culturally responsive care for Black youth
partners.what: Wanasah's clinicians share the background of the young people they treat. The approach is built on care that is culturally responsive, close to home, and free of the barriers that keep families from asking for help.
partners.why: Namarig Ahmed grew up in Regent Park. As she tells it, when she asked local services who was specifically supporting Black youth with their mental health, she could not find anyone who was. She and co-founder Dr. Leslie Shanks built an agency where mothers are brought in first and young people are trained up into staff roles. Namarig has said Wanasah turns down grants that would pull them off mission.
partners.funding: Wanasah secured what grassroots organizations rarely do: $100,000 in core funding from Ontario's Ministry of Health, following a $400,000 federal investment in Black-centric, trauma-responsive services in Regent Park. They integrated with Unity Health at St. Michael's Hospital, added a counsellor and a trusted psychiatrist to the team, and consulted on Toronto Foundation's Vital Signs report. They report a group of 50 youth ambassadors, several of whom have become staff. In June 2025 Namarig Ahmed received the King Charles III Coronation Medal from the Governor General.
